PEAS & BEANS

BEAN, BROAD
SUM / AUT
14–26 WEEKS
DIFFICULTY
EASY

One of the first crops off the plot each summer.

Broad beans are among the most dependable and useful garden crops. They are hardier than peas, will tolerate heavier soils than many beans, and can give fresh pods at a time when there is still relatively little else to pick. Autumn-sown plants often come through the winter and race away in early spring, while spring sowings provide the main summer crop. Each seed may produce several square-stemmed shoots, followed by scented black-and-white flowers and large pods containing green, white or sometimes reddish beans. Pick them young for the sweetest flavour; if left longer they become starchier but can be dried and stored as a useful winter food.

RECOMMENDED VARIETIES
TYPE	VARIETY	NOTES
Dwarf	The Sutton (White)	The best-known dwarf broad bean, useful for small or windy gardens and for growing under cloches.
Longpod	Aquadulce Claudia (White)	A popular longpod for autumn sowing and overwintering.
	Bunyard'S Exhibition (White)	Traditional longpod broad bean with white seeds, suitable for cooking fresh or freezing.
	Masterpiece Longpod (Green)	A green-seeded longpod with fine flavour.
	Imperial Green Longpod (Green)	Tall, green-seeded broad bean with long pods, suitable for a main crop.
KEY RISKS
BLACK BEAN APHID
Black aphids cluster on soft tips, especially on spring-sown broad beans.
CHOCOLATE SPOT
Small chocolate-brown spots appear on leaves, with dark streaks along the stems; pods and seeds may also be marked.
NO PODS
Flowers fall without forming pods.
PEA AND BEAN WEEVIL
U-shaped notches mark young leaves; seedlings may be badly damaged.

PEAS & BEANS

BEAN, BROAD

Rich soil, without waterlogging.

Moisture-retentive, free-draining ground suits broad beans.

Support tall varieties.

Stakes and strings keep plants upright in wind.

SOIL & PREPARATION
1
Choose sunny, moisture-retentive but free-draining ground where beans did not grow last year. Avoid waterlogging; lime very acid soil towards pH 6.5.
2
Ground enriched for a previous crop is ideal. Add compost or well-rotted manure in autumn if soil is poor.
SOWING & PLANTING
1
Sow large beans

Sow into prepared soil. Add spare seeds at row ends to provide seedlings for gaps.

2
Establish a double row

Grow two rows as a pair, with a wider gap before the next pair. Support tall varieties with stakes and strings in windy gardens.

Seed depth: 5 cm
Within each row pair: 25 cm between the two rows of a pair
Between row pairs: 60 cm between double rows
Plants: 20 cm between plants

Cold, heavy soil or mice: start in pots or modules under glass and set out when conditions improve.

Sow hardy varieties in late autumn only in mild districts. On cold or wet ground, wait until spring; pots or modules under glass are useful where mice threaten direct sowings.
LOOKING AFTER THE CROP
1
Weed young rows and earth stems up lightly to steady them. Support tall varieties in windy gardens with stakes and strings; dwarfs usually need little support.
2
Water thoroughly in dry weather from flowering and while pods swell. Mulch between plants to conserve moisture.
3
Pinch out soft tops at full flower or when the first pods form to discourage black bean aphid. Cook the tender tops like spinach.
4
After cropping, cut stems at the base, leaving roots and nodules in the soil. Compost the chopped stems.
HARVESTING
•
Pick regularly before pods become large and leathery. Very small pods with pea-sized beans can be cooked whole.
•
For shelling, pick when beans show clearly through the pods, before their attachment scars turn dark. Remove pods with a sharp downward twist.
•
For dried winter beans, let pods mature and dry on the plant if weather allows, then finish drying in an airy place before shelling and storing.
PESTS & DISEASES
PEST / DISEASE	SIGNS	CONTROL
Black Bean Aphid	Black colonies on soft growth.	Pinch infested tips; squash colonies; allow predators.
Chocolate Spot	Brown spots on leaves and stems.	Remove severe attacks; improve spacing and rotate.
No Pods	Flowers fall without pods.	Mulch and water roots well from flowering.
Pea And Bean Weevil	Notches in young leaf edges.	Water seedlings in drought; protect with fine mesh.
Birds	Torn pods	Protect seed and seedlings with netting or guards.
Mice	Seeds or seedlings vanish overnight.	Trap mice; raise seed in modules; protect sowings.
Bean Seed Fly	Tunnelled seeds and seedlings.	Remove damaged seedlings; plant module-raised beans.
Foot Rot And Root Rot	Dark, rotting roots and stem bases.	Remove affected plants; improve drainage; rotate.
FINAL TIPS
Sow spare seeds to fill gaps.
Wide rows of tall beans can shelter lower follow-on crops.

PEAS & BEANS

BEAN, FRENCH
SUM / AUT
8–12 WEEKS
DIFFICULTY
EASY

Dwarf or climbing, they crop over a long season.

French beans are tender summer beans, grown for crisp young pods, fresh shelled flageolets or fully ripened dried haricots. They are far less hardy than broad beans and should not be rushed into cold soil, but once the weather is warm they are quick, colourful and productive. Dwarf types crop earliest and need no formal supports, although their low pods can be dirtied by rain or damaged by slugs. Climbing types take more work to set up, but they keep the pods off the soil, reduce bending at picking time and can crop for longer.

SOW
May – Jun
HARVEST
Jul – Sep
GERMINATION
7–14 days

5 cm
ROW SPACING
45 cm between rows
PLANT SPACING
10 cm between plants
YIELD (3 M ROW)
bush: 3.6 kg; climbing: 5.4 kg
READY IN
About 8–12 weeks from sowing

1 = LOW   5 = HIGH

4/5

RECOMMENDED VARIETIES
TYPE	VARIETY	NOTES
Green	Cropper Teepee	The Pencil-pods are large with white seeds - a reliable heavy-cropping variety with good disease resistance.
	Masterpiece	Another old favourite Flat-pod - suitable for early sowing.
	Canadian Wonder	A heavy cropping Flat-pod - once popular but no longer to be found in all the catalogues.
	Tendergreen	Perhaps the most popular of all the Pencil-podded types, and justly so.
	Hunter	The pods are long, wide, straight and stringless - this high-yielding climber is widely available.
	Annabel	A compact variety which bears masses of thin stringless pods.
KEY RISKS
BLACK BEAN APHID
Black bean aphids can cluster on French-bean shoots in summer.
NO PODS
French beans may drop flowers or set few pods when roots are dry, especially in hot weather.
PEA AND BEAN WEEVIL
Tell-tale signs are U-shaped notches around the edges of young pea or bean leaves, and sometimes damage to the growing centres.
BIRDS
Birds can be a nuisance in several ways.

PEAS & BEANS

BEAN, FRENCH

Wait for warmth.

Cold, wet ground can rot seed; plant out after frost danger has passed.

Protect young seedlings.

Keep beds clean and weed-free, and watch for slugs.

SOIL & PREPARATION
1
Choose a warm, sheltered, sunny site with light, well-drained soil. Add compost or well-rotted manure; avoid cold, wet clay and lime only if soil is too acid.
2
Use ground where beans did not grow last year. Climbing beans need richer, moisture-retentive soil than dwarfs: enrich a trench or planting strip where ground is poor.
SOWING & PLANTING
1
Sow in warm soil

After frost risk, sow two beans per station in warm soil. For an early start, raise under glass, harden off and plant out.

2
Keep the strongest

Remove the weaker seedling. Dwarf types grow in rows or blocks; put supports in place early for climbing types.

Seed depth: 5 cm
Dwarf rows: 45 cm between rows
Close-spaced dwarf rows: plants: 10 cm between plants
Dwarf blocks: plants: 15 cm each way
Climbing supports: 15 cm between canes; retain one plant per cane
Sow outdoors from late May; repeat in late June or early July.
For early crops, warm soil under cloches in March, sow in April; uncover in late May.
LOOKING AFTER THE CROP
1
Protect seedlings from slugs; keep beds clean and weed-free, especially below low dwarf pods.
2
Dwarf varieties normally need no support. Give climbers canes, netting, wigwams or strings early; guide wandering shoots onto them.
3
Water regularly in dry weather from flowering onwards. Steady root moisture and warmth matter more than spraying flowers.
4
Water and use an organic liquid feed after the first flush of pods to encourage a smaller second crop.
HARVESTING
•
Pick tender green pods every few days before the beans inside swell. Search carefully for pods hidden in climbing foliage.
•
Dwarfs usually crop first, for about four to six weeks; replace tired plants with a later sowing. Climbers may crop for six to ten weeks with regular picking and watering.
•
For dried haricots, let pods ripen and turn straw-coloured. Finish drying plants in an airy shed if needed, then shell and dry beans fully before storing airtight.
PESTS & DISEASES
PEST / DISEASE	SIGNS	CONTROL
Black Bean Aphid	Black colonies on soft growth.	Squash damaging colonies; allow predators.
No Pods	Flowers fall without pods.	Mulch and water roots well from flowering.
Pea And Bean Weevil	Notches in young leaf edges.	Water seedlings in drought; protect with fine mesh.
Birds	Torn pods	Protect seed and seedlings with netting, guards, twigs or black cotton.
Mice	Missing seed or seedlings before establishment.	Trap mice; raise seed in modules; protect sowings.
Halo Blight	Leaf spots with yellow halos.	Remove diseased plants; use clean seed; rotate.
Bean Seed Fly	Tunnelled seeds and seedlings.	Remove damaged seedlings; plant module-raised beans.
FINAL TIPS
Pick before beans swell inside pods.
Give climbers supports at sowing or planting time.

FRUITING CROPS

COURGETTES AND MARROWS
SUM / AUT
8–14 WEEKS
DIFFICULTY
NOT DIFFICULT

One or two plants are plenty for most kitchens.

Courgettes and marrows are the same general crop at different stages of use: courgettes are picked young, firm and tender, while marrows are allowed to grow larger and can be eaten fresh or stored. Modern courgette varieties are bred to keep producing small fruits, and a well-grown plant in summer warmth can be almost overwhelming, often giving several courgettes each week.

QUICK FACTS
SOW
Apr – Jun
HARVEST
Jul – Oct
GERMINATION
5–8 days
DEPTH
Indoors: 1.5 cm; direct outdoors: 2.5 cm
ROW SPACING
Courgettes and bush marrows: at least 90 cm between planting sites in each direction; trailing marrows: at least 150 cm.
PLANT SPACING
one plant per prepared pocket or station
YIELD PER PLANT
marrows: 4 mature marrows, or many more immature courgettes from true courgette varieties; courgettes: Several fruits per week at peak growth; total crop varies with season and picking
READY IN
About 8–14 weeks from sowing; pick courgettes young
CORE NEEDS
1 = LOW   5 = HIGH
SUN
4/5
WATER
5/5
NUTRITION
5/5

SOW

RECOMMENDED VARIETIES
TYPE	VARIETY	NOTES
Courgette	Early Gem F1	Early and prolific; a favourite green courgette, often ready in about 60 days.
	Supremo	A dark green courgette for regular young-fruit harvesting.
	Diamant F1	A green-fruited hybrid, sometimes translated as Diamond in seed listings.
	Onyx F1	A dark, glossy green hybrid courgette with long, cylindrical fruit.
	Rondo Di Nizza	Round green courgettes; productive and good for stuffing when picked young.
	Zucchini	The classic dark green courgette, producing freely for salads or cooked dishes.
KEY RISKS
SLUGS
Slugs chew seedlings, especially in cold, wet weather.
MILDEW
White powder coats leaves, often late in the season.
POOR POLLINATION
If fruitlets yellow, wither or fail to swell, pollination may be poor.
FRUIT ROT
Fruit resting on wet soil may soften and rot.

FRUITING CROPS

COURGETTES AND MARROWS

Warmth and moisture drive growth.

Plant after frost and avoid cold, wet starts or drought checks.

SOIL & PREPARATION
1
Use a warm, sunny, sheltered site with rich, moisture-retentive but well-drained soil. Prepare compost-rich planting pockets.
2
Mulch generously and leave enough room for the chosen bush or trailing type. Avoid poorly drained ground.
SOWING & PLANTING
1
Sow on edge

Sow singly in warm pots or modules, with the seed on edge. Keep compost lightly moist; cold, wet compost can rot the seed.

2
Keep one strong plant

Harden off and plant after frost risk. For direct sowing in warm soil, sow two or three per station and keep the strongest.

Seed depth by route: Indoors: 1.5 cm; direct outdoors: 2.5 cm
Spacing by type: Courgettes and bush marrows: at least 90 cm between planting sites in each direction; trailing marrows: at least 150 cm.
Final plants: one plant per prepared pocket or station
Start warm indoor sowings in late April and plant after frost risk. Direct sowing is safer in warm late-May or June soil; temporary fleece helps establishment.
LOOKING AFTER THE CROP
1
Water deeply around the roots and mulch with compost to keep growth steady. Avoid prolonged leaf wetness.
2
Allow pollinators access. If fruit set is poor, transfer pollen from a male flower to the centre of a female flower, which has a small fruit behind it.
3
Use strong supports for trailing marrows, tying stems gently. Support heavy fruit separately; restrict unwanted extension if needed.
HARVESTING
•
Cut courgettes young, often at 10–15 cm, daily or every other day in warm weather. Leave a short stem rather than snapping fruit off.
•
Pick marrows tender for immediate use, or let selected storage fruits develop hard skins before frost. Handle gently and keep dry.
•
Discard unusually bitter fruit. Wear gloves or long sleeves if stems irritate your skin; flowers can also be used in the kitchen.
PESTS & DISEASES
PEST / DISEASE	SIGNS	CONTROL
Slugs	Young plants are chewed.	Protect establishment; inspect and hand-pick in damp weather.
Mildew	White powder on older leaves.	Keep roots moist; remove badly affected leaves as needed.
Poor Pollination	Fruitlets yellow, wither or fail to swell.	Allow insect access; hand-pollinate where necessary.
Fruit Rot	Fruit softens where it touches wet ground.	Lift onto a clean support; remove rotten fruit.
Cucumber Mosaic Virus	Mottled, puckered leaves; stunted growth.	Remove infected plants; clear weed hosts and monitor aphids.
Bitterness	Fruit tastes unusually bitter.	Discard bitter fruit; do not try to make it safe by cooking.
Root Rot	Wilting; dark, decaying roots.	Remove collapsed plants; improve drainage and avoid cold wet roots.
FINAL TIPS
Raise developing marrows on a clean tile or board to keep their skins dry and sound.
Remove misshapen first fruits and keep picking young courgettes to encourage the next crop.

COURGETTES AND MARROWS

Warmth and moisture drive growth.

Plant after frost and avoid cold, wet starts or drought checks.

SOIL & PREPARATION
1
Use a warm, sunny, sheltered site with rich, moisture-retentive but well-drained soil. Prepare compost-rich planting pockets.
2
Mulch generously and leave enough room for the chosen bush or trailing type. Avoid poorly drained ground.
SOWING & PLANTING
1
Sow on edge

Sow singly in warm pots or modules, with the seed on edge. Keep compost lightly moist; cold, wet compost can rot the seed.

2
Keep one strong plant

Harden off and plant after frost risk. For direct sowing in warm soil, sow two or three per station and keep the strongest.

Seed depth by route: Indoors: 5/8 in.; direct outdoors: 1 in.
Spacing by type: Courgettes and bush marrows: at least 3 ft between planting sites in each direction; trailing marrows: at least 5 ft.
Final plants: one plant per prepared pocket or station
Start warm indoor sowings in late April and plant after frost risk. Direct sowing is safer in warm late-May or June soil; temporary fleece helps establishment.
LOOKING AFTER THE CROP
1
Water deeply around the roots and mulch with compost to keep growth steady. Avoid prolonged leaf wetness.
2
Allow pollinators access. If fruit set is poor, transfer pollen from a male flower to the centre of a female flower, which has a small fruit behind it.
3
Use strong supports for trailing marrows, tying stems gently. Support heavy fruit separately; restrict unwanted extension if needed.
HARVESTING
•
Cut courgettes young, often at 4–6 in., daily or every other day in warm weather. Leave a short stem rather than snapping fruit off.
•
Pick marrows tender for immediate use, or let selected storage fruits develop hard skins before frost. Handle gently and keep dry.
•
Discard unusually bitter fruit. Wear gloves or long sleeves if stems irritate your skin; flowers can also be used in the kitchen.
PESTS & DISEASES
PEST / DISEASE	SIGNS	CONTROL
Slugs	Young plants are chewed.	Protect establishment; inspect and hand-pick in damp weather.
Mildew	White powder on older leaves.	Keep roots moist; remove badly affected leaves as needed.
Poor Pollination	Fruitlets yellow, wither or fail to swell.	Allow insect access; hand-pollinate where necessary.
Fruit Rot	Fruit softens where it touches wet ground.	Lift onto a clean support; remove rotten fruit.
Cucumber Mosaic Virus	Mottled, puckered leaves; stunted growth.	Remove infected plants; clear weed hosts and monitor aphids.
Bitterness	Fruit tastes unusually bitter.	Discard bitter fruit; do not try to make it safe by cooking.
Root Rot	Wilting; dark, decaying roots.	Remove collapsed plants; improve drainage and avoid cold wet roots.
FINAL TIPS
Raise developing marrows on a clean tile or board to keep their skins dry and sound.
Remove misshapen first fruits and keep picking young courgettes to encourage the next crop.

ONION FAMILY

GARLIC

Plant healthy cloves in good drainage.

Named planting stock gives a more predictable crop than kitchen bulbs.

Lift and dry bulbs at maturity.

Careful handling and thorough drying help garlic keep.

SOIL & PREPARATION
1
Choose an open, sunny site with fertile, well-drained soil. Add compost or well-rotted manure, but avoid stagnant winter wet.
2
A compost top-dressing helps retain moisture; keep it clear of emerging shoots.
SOWING & PLANTING
1
Set a clove upright

Split a sound bulb shortly before planting. Choose large outside cloves and set each one pointed end upwards.

2
Cover the clove tip

Cover the pointed tip with soil and firm around the clove. Deeper planting suits light soil, not heavy ground.

Soil above clove tip: Cover the pointed clove tip with 2.5 cm of soil; deeper planting is suitable in light soil, not heavy soil
Rows / blocks: 30 cm between rows
Cloves: Ordinary garlic: 15 cm apart; elephant garlic: about 30 cm apart
Plant named healthy stock at the season recommended for the variety, usually autumn; some varieties suit late winter or early spring. Save only sound bulbs from healthy crops.
LOOKING AFTER THE CROP
1
Keep weeds down through winter and spring. Slow winter shoots are normal; growth strengthens as conditions warm.
2
Water roots in dry weather while bulbs grow; stop as mature foliage yellows. Cut tender hardneck scapes once buds form.
HARVESTING
•
Use green garlic whole in late spring. Check mature bulbs from June and lift as foliage yellows, before skins break down.
•
Loosen soil, lift gently and brush off dirt without washing. Cure for two to four weeks in dry, airy shelter, then store cool and dry.
•
Severe rust can bring harvest forward. Elephant garlic needs more room and a longer season; judge maturity from the plant and bulb.
PESTS & DISEASES
PEST / DISEASE	SIGNS	CONTROL
White Rot	White mould and decay at bulb bases.	Remove diseased plants; keep alliums off infected ground.
Allium Leaf Miner	White puncture rows; internal maggots or pupae.	Mesh during fly activity; remove infested plants and debris.
Rust	Orange pustules; leaves yellow early.	Avoid crowding and excess nitrogen; clear affected debris.
Birds Or Frost Lifting Cloves	Cloves are pulled up or frost-heaved.	Cover tips at planting; firm and replant lifted cloves.
Poor Storage	Bulbs rot or sprout in store.	Lift on time, handle gently and dry thoroughly.
Stem & Bulb Eelworm	Swollen, distorted growth; soft bases.	Confirm diagnosis; remove plants and avoid moving affected soil.
FINAL TIPS
Softneck types usually store longer; use hardnecks earlier and enjoy their edible scapes.
Elephant garlic is a leek relative with large, mild cloves, so give it extra room.

RADISH
SPR / SUM / AUT
3–12 WEEKS
DIFFICULTY
EASY

From sowing to salad bowl in a matter of weeks.

Radishes are among the fastest root crops and deserve a place for their speed alone: spring sowings can give mild, juicy roots when few other outdoor crops are ready. They are useful in odd corners, window boxes, under protection, or as a quick crop between slower vegetables. The familiar small red and red-white radishes are best eaten young, before heat, age or drought makes them hot, woody, hollow or soft. Winter radishes are a more substantial crop: they include white, pink, black and red-white types, grow for much longer, and can be grated, pickled, braised, stir-fried or stored in cool damp conditions after lifting in autumn.

ROOT CROPS

RADISH

Sun in spring; light shade in summer.

Hot, dry conditions make roots hotter and woodier.

Thin only where needed.

Pull the largest roots first and let smaller ones grow on.

Do not sow winter radishes too early.

They need to grow steadily into autumn, not bolt in summer.

SOIL & PREPARATION
1
Use rich, damp soil with a little compost and a fine tilth for rapid, tender growth.
2
Choose sun in spring and light shade in summer. Lime acid soil if needed; give winter radishes humus-rich drainage.
SOWING & PLANTING
1
Sow salad radishes

Sow a short drill thinly and cover lightly. Repeat small sowings for succession.

2
Leave room to grow

Leave room between salad radishes; thin crowded seedlings.

Seed depth: Salad radishes: 1 cm; winter and oriental radishes: about 2 cm.
Salad rows: 15 cm between rows
Winter rows: 15 cm between rows
Salad plants: Sow or thin to 2.5-5 cm apart.
Oriental plants: Sow or thin to 15-20 cm apart, depending on variety.
Winter plants: Sow or thin to 15-20 cm apart, depending on variety.

For a small patch, broadcast seed and rake it in. Winter radishes: sow in July or early August to reduce bolting.

Sow small batches every fortnight. Early sowings can go under cloches, glass or plastic; late-winter sowing is for favourable areas.
After May, cabbage root fly damage is more likely. Summer heat makes rapid growth harder to maintain.
LOOKING AFTER THE CROP
1
Keep rows moist and weed-free. Quick, uninterrupted growth is the secret of crisp, mild radishes; water particularly as roots swell.
2
Thin only where needed. Pull the largest summer roots first, letting smaller ones grow on, but do not leave any too long.
3
Protect young leaves from flea beetle with fine mesh or fleece. Clear quick crops promptly for the next crop.
HARVESTING
•
Pull spring and summer radishes while small, crisp and mildly flavoured. French Breakfast types are best before they become finger-thick and tough.
•
Many spring varieties take 40-50 days; very quick crops may be ready in three to four weeks in good conditions. Pull surplus roots rather than leaving them to turn woody or hollow.
•
Lift winter radishes in October or November before hard frost, or leave hardy kinds in the ground where frost is not severe. Store lifted roots cool and damp, for example in sand.
PESTS & DISEASES
PEST / DISEASE	SIGNS	CONTROL
Flea Beetle	Shot-holed leaves.	Keep moist; use fine mesh.
Bolting	Early flowers; poor roots.	Sow winter radishes from July onwards.
Cabbage Root Fly	Roots tunnelled by maggots.	Use mesh; trim minor root damage.
Woody Or Hollow Roots	Hot, woody or hollow roots.	Water evenly; thin and harvest promptly.
Acid Soil	Poor growth in acid soil.	Test soil; lime only where needed.
Slugs And Snails	Chewed seedlings; slime trails.	Check after dark; hand-pick around seedlings.
FINAL TIPS
Sow winter radishes in July or early August, not spring.
Clear quick crops promptly for the next crop.
